newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan poll pressure mounts, analysts split on date.
newsitem.headline: Japan poll pressure mounts, analysts split on date.

text.p: Political pressure is mounting on Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto to call a general election this autumn, but local analysts share no consensus on the timing of a vote.
A Reuters Financial Television survey of 10 Japan-based economic and political analysts shows opinion split down the middle on whether Hashimoto will call polls for the 500-seat Lower House in 1996.
A report in the Mainichi Shimbun newspaper on Thursday said Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) had urged him to dissolve parliament in October and hold elections this year.

According to the RFTV survey, conducted from Monday to Thursday, those who expect a 1996 vote cite dwindling LDP coffers, political disarray in the other two parties in the ruling coalition and LDP concerns about political fallout from a planned rise in Japan's consumption tax next April to five percent from the current three percent.
But the reasons to put off an election until next year are just as strong, some analysts say.

They said the government faces possible presentation of a supplementary budget for the fiscal year to next March, a worsening fiscal situation and a non-binding referendum on the U.S. military presence in the southern island of Okinawa on September 8 -- plus tenuous support for the Hashimoto cabinet.
"Prime Minister Hashimoto (and the LDP) need to wait to increase his popularity within the next year," said Teizo Taya, director of Daiwa Institute of Research.
An election for the Lower House must be called by July 1997.
According to the survey, while there is uncertainty about the timing, nearly all local analysts believe the current coalition will not survive an election, whenever it is held.
The LDP's coalition partners, the Social Democratic Party and New Party Sakigake, have made overtures this week about forming a new political party in September.
But analysts say this is a sign of desperation rather than potential strength before a possible election.
"The Socialists will be wiped out in the next vote," said John Neuffer, a senior fellow at Mitsui Marine Research.
The key issue in the election may be the planned rise in the consumption tax, which the opposition Shinshinto and some members of LDP have proposed postponing.
Nine of the 10 analysts surveyed do not expect the rise to be postponed, although an extension of special income tax cuts to next year may be offered instead.
"There may be a lot of horse trading, but the (Finance Ministry ) will fight tooth and nail to see the hike implemented," said Andrew Shipley of Schroders Japan Ltd.

The analysts surveyed were Citibank NA, Daiwa Institute of Research, Deutsche Bank Capital Markets (Asia), the Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan, Merrill Lynch Japan, Mitsui Marine Research Institute, Salomon Brothers Asia, Sanyo Investment Research, Schroders Japan and Technical Data Corp.
